voiceInstructions: Warm, precise American English biology teacher. Read genotype symbols, allele notation, sequence direction and probability carefully. Speak every sentence fully, with short pauses before predictions and worked answers. Do not add or omit words.
title: Genetics: Pedigrees, Maps and Molecular Data
subject: Biology
scope: NEET 2026 Biology Unit 7 problem-solving supplement: pedigree probabilities, X-linked inheritance, linkage, recombination, three-point mapping, sequence orientation, gene regulation and Hardy–Weinberg interpretation. Build on the existing Genetics and Evolution foundation class. Original teaching and practice; no official PYQs or calibrated exam predictions.

sources.title: OpenStax Biology 2e: DNA Structure and Function

chapters.title: Read the pedigree model before the symbols
chapters.formula: Autosomal recessive: aa affected; Aa × Aa → 1/4 aa
points: State the inheritance model and penetrance assumptions.
Use sex, parent-to-child transmission and generations as evidence.
Separate a compatible pattern from proof of a diagnosis.
chapters.script: Welcome to a problem-solving supplement for Genetics and Evolution. We will use pedigrees, linkage data and sequence evidence, then make each assumption visible. A pedigree is a record of family relationships and a trait, not a diagnosis by itself. Before calculating, state a model: for example, a fully penetrant autosomal recessive allele with a rare disease allele. In that model, two unaffected carrier parents, A a and A a, have an affected child a a with probability one quarter in each pregnancy. The chance is the same for every pregnancy; earlier children do not change it. An affected child with unaffected parents can fit this model, but other explanations may also fit incomplete data. Track the evidence without claiming that one small pedigree proves the mode of inheritance. Ask which observations distinguish the models, and which do not.

chapters.title: Conditional carrier probability
chapters.formula: Unaffected child of Aa × Aa: P(Aa | unaffected) = 2/3
points: List the three unaffected genotypes: AA, Aa and Aa.
Condition on the given observation before calculating risk.
Multiply independent risks along the stated family path.
chapters.script: Here is a common conditional-probability trap. For two carrier parents, the four equally likely child outcomes are A A, A a, A a and a a. If a sibling is known to be unaffected, remove the affected a a outcome from the denominator. Two of the remaining three outcomes are carriers, so the conditional carrier probability is two thirds, not one half. Suppose that sibling has a child with an unrelated partner whose carrier probability is specified as one in fifty. Under the stated assumptions, the affected-child probability is two thirds times one fiftieth times one quarter, which simplifies to one in three hundred. The partner risk is a question input; do not invent a population frequency. In every pedigree problem, write the conditioning information first, then count compatible genotypes, then multiply only independent transmission events.

chapters.title: Distinguish X-linked recessive transmission
chapters.formula: Carrier mother × unaffected father: each son has 1/2 risk
points: A son receives a Y chromosome from his father.
A daughter receives her father's X chromosome.
A carrier mother transmits either X allele with probability 1/2.
chapters.script: For an X-linked recessive model, write the two sex chromosomes for each parent and child. A son receives his Y chromosome from his father and his single X chromosome from his mother. If the mother is a carrier, each son has a one-half probability of receiving the variant X. An unaffected father does not transmit his X chromosome to a son, so father-to-son transmission is not expected under this model. A daughter receives her father's X chromosome; with an unaffected father, one variant X from a carrier mother usually makes her a carrier rather than affected. These statements rely on the specified simple model, ordinary chromosome transmission and full penetrance. A pedigree can be small, and a rare trait may be absent by chance in one branch. Do not label a trait X-linked only because more affected people happen to be male. Look for the complete transmission pattern.

chapters.title: Estimate recombination from a testcross
points: In a testcross, offspring classes reflect heterozygote gametes.
Combine both recombinant classes in the numerator.
A small two-locus value estimates map distance in centimorgans.
chapters.script: In a testcross, a double heterozygote is crossed with a homozygous recessive tester. If the tester contributes only recessive alleles, offspring classes reveal the gametes made by the heterozygote. Suppose thirty-six of two hundred forty offspring are recombinant across the two loci. The estimated recombination frequency is thirty-six divided by two hundred forty, or fifteen percent. For a short interval, this is conventionally reported as about fifteen map units, or fifteen centimorgans. It is an estimate from sampled offspring, so a larger sample generally gives a more stable estimate. Recombination frequency cannot exceed fifty percent in the usual two-locus scoring, because independent assortment also produces half recombinant classes. Multiple crossovers can restore parental allele combinations and make long physical distances appear smaller. Therefore, do not interpret a measured percentage as an exact physical distance across every interval.

chapters.title: Keep allele phase visible
chapters.formula: AB/ab: parental gametes AB, ab; recombinants Ab, aB
points: Write the two homologous chromosomes before listing gametes.
Parental phase identifies which allele combinations are nonrecombinant.
Split each class total equally only under a stated symmetry model.
chapters.script: The same genotype letters can hide different chromosome arrangements. In coupling phase, write A B slash a b: the dominant alleles are together on one homolog. In repulsion phase, write A b slash a B: each homolog carries one dominant and one recessive allele. A testcross identifies which offspring classes are common parental types and which are recombinant types, but phase must be recorded to interpret them. If coupling-phase recombination frequency is twenty percent and reciprocal classes are equally frequent, the total parental fraction is eighty percent, so each parental gamete class is forty percent. The total recombinant fraction is twenty percent, so each recombinant class is ten percent. Those paired expectations rely on the simple symmetric model. Do not call A B recombinant merely because it contains two capital letters. It is parental in coupling and recombinant in repulsion.

chapters.title: Infer gene order with three-point data
chapters.formula: Parentals: ABC, abc · double crossovers: AbC, aBc
points: Identify the two most frequent parental and least frequent double-crossover classes.
Compare each pair to find the allele that switches in the middle locus.
Count double crossovers in both adjacent interval estimates.
chapters.script: Three-point testcross data can reveal gene order and expose crossovers missed by a two-point estimate. Consider one thousand offspring. The two largest classes are A B C with four hundred ten and a b c with four hundred five. Treat these as the parental classes. The two smallest are A b C and a B c, one each, so they are the double crossovers. Compare A B C with A b C: only the B allele changes. Compare a b c with a B c: again only B changes. Therefore B is the middle locus, and the order is A, B, C. If the single-crossover classes between A and B total one hundred forty-five, that interval count becomes one hundred forty-seven after adding both double crossovers, or fourteen point seven percent. If the B to C single-crossover classes total thirty-eight, include the same two double crossovers to get four percent. Keep the intervals separate before summing map length.

chapters.title: Read a coding strand and a frameshift
chapters.formula: Coding DNA 5′ ATG GAA TTT TGA 3′ → mRNA 5′ AUG GAA UUU UGA 3′
points: The coding strand matches mRNA except T is replaced by U.
Translation reads codons in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
A one-base insertion or deletion changes the downstream frame.
chapters.script: Sequence questions depend on strand labels and direction. If a coding DNA strand is written five-prime A T G, G A A, T T T, T G A three-prime, the messenger RNA has the same sequence with U in place of T: A U G, G A A, U U U, U G A. Translation reads the RNA in groups of three from its five-prime end. These codons specify methionine, glutamate, phenylalanine and then a stop signal. The template strand is complementary and antiparallel, so do not copy it directly as the coding sequence. A substitution may change one codon, create a stop, or be synonymous, depending on the code. Inserting or deleting one nucleotide usually shifts the reading frame for downstream codons. Inserting or deleting three nucleotides preserves the frame but can add or remove an amino acid. Always mark the strand, direction and frame before translating.

chapters.title: Combine gene regulation and population evidence
points: For a recessive phenotype, q² gives the affected frequency under the model.
Use p = 1 − q, then calculate heterozygotes as 2pq.
An observed deviation alone does not identify its cause.
chapters.script: Finish by separating a molecular regulation model from a population-frequency model. In the lac operon example, lactose-derived allolactose binds the repressor and reduces its attachment to the operator. This permits transcription when the other required conditions are present; it does not guarantee the same expression in every cell context. For a separate Hardy–Weinberg calculation, suppose a fully recessive phenotype occurs at frequency nine percent in a population at equilibrium. Under that model, q squared equals zero point zero nine, so q is zero point three and p is zero point seven. The expected heterozygote frequency is two p q, or zero point four two. This prediction assumes random mating at the locus and no relevant selection, migration, mutation or drift that disrupts the model. A measured difference may reflect sampling, model violations or genotyping error. It does not by itself identify which evolutionary force acted. State assumptions before interpreting a frequency.

quiz.question: Under a fully penetrant autosomal recessive model, which genotype is affected?
options: Any genotype with a dominant allele
quiz.explanation: Only aa is homozygous recessive in this stated model. Carrier Aa individuals are unaffected under the full-penetrance assumption.

quiz.question: Two carrier parents have an affected child under the simple autosomal recessive model. What is the probability their next child is affected?
quiz.explanation: Each pregnancy is an independent transmission event with a 1/4 probability of aa. The previous child's genotype does not change that probability.

quiz.question: An unaffected sibling of an affected child from Aa × Aa parents is known to be unaffected. What is the sibling's carrier probability?
quiz.explanation: Condition on the three unaffected outcomes AA, Aa and Aa. Two of those three are carriers, giving 2/3.

quiz.question: A 2/3 carrier-risk sibling has a child with a partner known to have a 1/50 carrier probability. Under the same recessive model, what is the affected-child risk?
quiz.explanation: Multiply the carrier probabilities and the 1/4 affected probability: (2/3)(1/50)(1/4) = 1/300.

quiz.question: In a simple X-linked recessive model, which parent supplies a son's X chromosome?
quiz.explanation: A typical son inherits a Y chromosome from his father and an X chromosome from his mother. Thus his X-linked allele comes from the mother.

quiz.question: Thirty-six of 240 testcross offspring are recombinant. What is the estimated recombination frequency?
quiz.explanation: 36/240 × 100% = 15%. For a short interval this is conventionally about 15 cM.

quiz.question: A 15% recombination estimate across a short interval is conventionally reported as approximately:
quiz.explanation: For a short interval, one percentage point of recombination is conventionally about one centimorgan. Multiple crossovers limit this approximation over longer distances.

quiz.question: For an AB/ab heterozygote with 20% recombination and equal reciprocal classes, what is the frequency of each recombinant gamete?
quiz.explanation: The 20% total recombinant fraction is divided equally between Ab and aB under the stated symmetry model, so each is 10%.

quiz.question: Which is a parental gamete for a coupling-phase AB/ab heterozygote?
quiz.explanation: The parental allele combinations are those on the original homologues: AB and ab. Ab and aB are recombinant combinations.

quiz.question: In a three-point cross, parental classes are ABC and abc while the least frequent classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene is in the middle?
quiz.explanation: Each double-crossover class differs from its corresponding parental class only at B, identifying B as the middle locus.

quiz.question: For the B–C interval in the narrated dataset, 38 single crossovers and two double crossovers occur among 1,000 offspring. What is the map estimate?
quiz.explanation: Include double crossovers in the B–C interval: (38 + 2)/1000 × 100 = 4.0 cM.

quiz.question: What mRNA is transcribed from the coding DNA strand 5′-ATG GAA TTT TGA-3′?
quiz.explanation: The coding-strand sequence matches the mRNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction, with uracil in place of thymine.

quiz.question: A one-nucleotide deletion within a coding region most commonly causes which effect downstream?
options: A change to exactly one codon only
No change to the reading frame
A guaranteed amino-acid substitution at every position
quiz.explanation: A one-base deletion changes grouping into triplet codons downstream of the deletion. The specific protein outcome depends on sequence context and may encounter a stop.

quiz.question: In the lac operon model, allolactose most directly:
options: Binds the operator DNA as RNA polymerase
Binds the repressor and reduces its operator binding
quiz.explanation: Allolactose acts as an inducer by binding the repressor, reducing its ability to block transcription at the operator.

quiz.question: A recessive phenotype has frequency 0.09 at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What is the expected heterozygote frequency?
quiz.explanation: q² = 0.09 gives q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. The heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2(0.7)(0.3) = 0.42.

quiz.question: A population differs from Hardy–Weinberg expectations. What can be concluded from that deviation alone?
options: A single evolutionary force is identified
The model assumptions or sampling may need review; the cause is not uniquely identified
The allele frequency is necessarily zero
quiz.explanation: Deviation signals that the model fit or assumptions need examination, but it cannot by itself distinguish selection, migration, drift, nonrandom mating, mutation or measurement issues.
